title: 1 Kings 9:10–14
context: After twenty years of building the temple and the palace (compare 6:38; 7:1), Solomon gives Hiram king of Tyre twenty cities in Galilee in return for his supply of cedar, cypress and gold. Hiram is not pleased with them and calls them the land of Cabul, a name often said to sound like Hebrew for good-for-nothing. Hiram sends Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 8:2 speaks of cities Huram had given to Solomon, and interpreters harmonize the two accounts in different ways. The text does not explain the exact terms of the exchange, and readers should not supply more than it says. Both traditions read this as a historical notice about diplomacy and trade, without a theological fork.

verses.text: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the LORD’s house and the king’s house
verses.arminianNotes:
At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon built the LORD’s house and the king’s house, a new section begins. The figure matches seven years for the temple and thirteen for the palace (6:38; 7:1).

Arminian readers note that the long building period shows the scale of Solomon’s investment, and that the narrator now turns from God’s warning to the practical dealings of the kingdom, inviting readers to weigh them in its light.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator’s placement of these notices right after God’s warning invites readers to watch how Solomon’s reign unfolds against the standard just set, while recognizing that the notices themselves are descriptive.

Both traditions read this verse as a transition into administrative records.

verses.text: (now Hiram the king of Tyre had furnished Solomon with cedar trees and cypress trees, and with gold, according to all his desire), King Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar, cypress and gold as he wished, and Solomon gives Hiram twenty cities in Galilee. The exchange is part of their alliance.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s dealings with Hiram show international cooperation in building God’s house, and that the text simply reports the arrangement without passing judgment on it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 8:2 speaks of cities Huram gave to Solomon, which interpreters harmonize in different ways, for example by suggesting that Hiram later returned these cities; the text does not settle it.

Both traditions read the exchange as historical narrative and hold the harmonization with humility.

verses.text: Hiram came out of Tyre to see the cities which Solomon had given him; and they didn’t please him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram comes from Tyre to see the cities, and they do not please him. He is disappointed.

Arminian readers note that the narrative honestly records friction between allies, and that even successful partnerships involve disappointment and imperfect dealings, which Scripture does not hide.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator offers no explanation of why the cities did not please Hiram, and readers should resist supplying motives the text does not give, whether about Solomon’s fairness or Hiram’s expectations.

Both traditions see the verse as a realistic detail in the record of Solomon’s reign rather than a basis for doctrine.

verses.text: He said, “What cities are these which you have given me, my brother?” He called them the land of Cabul to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram asks what cities these are that Solomon has given him, calling him brother, and names them the land of Cabul. The WEB footnote says the name sounds like Hebrew for good-for-nothing.

Arminian readers note that Hiram’s courteous address as brother sits alongside his complaint, reflecting the language of treaty partners, and that the name preserves his dissatisfaction.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that a town called Cabul also appears in Asher’s territory (Joshua 19:27), and that the wordplay in the name is a memorable way of recording the episode; the precise background remains uncertain.

Both traditions read the verse as a historical notice without theological controversy.

verses.text: Hiram sent to the king one hundred twenty talents of gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hiram sends the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold. The WEB footnote estimates this at about 3.6 metric tons.

Arminian readers note that the text does not make clear whether this gold was payment for the cities, an earlier contribution, or a gift, and readers should not press the relationship beyond what the narrative states.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the same amount appears in the queen of Sheba’s gift (10:10), and that the narrative’s attention to gold builds a picture of Solomon’s wealth that the following chapters will set alongside the warning of Deuteronomy 17:17.

Both traditions read the notice descriptively and avoid speculation about the terms.
